claim: The specimen preserves a strikingly enlarged feathered crest on the head that extends from the caudal end of the skull to a position rostral to the nasal bone.
source: Among its diverse feather morphologies, this specimen also displays a strikingly enlarged feathered crest on the head that uniquely extends from the caudal end of the skull to a position rostral to the nasal bone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text describes the crest morphology and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for visual evidence.

claim: The densely packed rod-like melanosomes in the head crest feathers are estimated to have yielded from red to deep blue iridescent coloration.
source: The densely packed rod-like melanosomes are estimated to have yielded from red to deep blue iridescent coloration of the head feathers.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the estimated color range based on melanosome analysis.

claim: The shape and density of melanosomes may have increased the feather's structural strength.
source: The shape and density of these melanosomes also may have further increased the feather's structural strength.
evidence: The abstract states this as a potential function of the melanosome characteristics.

claim: The iridescent crest likely occurred on a male individual.
source: This occurrence on a likely male individual is highly suggestive of both a signaling function of the iridescent crest and a potential behavioral role in adjusting the angle of light incidence to control the display of this iridescent structural coloration.
evidence: The abstract states the individual is likely male, with further justification provided later in the manuscript.

claim: The iridescent crest had a signaling function.
source: This occurrence on a likely male individual is highly suggestive of both a signaling function of the iridescent crest and a potential behavioral role in adjusting the angle of light incidence to control the display of this iridescent structural coloration.
evidence: The abstract suggests a signaling function based on the presence of iridescence on a likely male individual.

claim: The bird may have behaviorally controlled the display of iridescent coloration by adjusting the angle of light incidence.
source: This occurrence on a likely male individual is highly suggestive of both a signaling function of the iridescent crest and a potential behavioral role in adjusting the angle of light incidence to control the display of this iridescent structural coloration.
evidence: The abstract suggests a potential behavioral role in controlling iridescent display.

claim: Melanosomes in fossil feathers have demonstrated the intertwined evolution of coloration with feather functions across display, thermoregulation, and other uses.
source: The recognition and study of melanosomes in fossil feathers of non-avialan dinosaurs and birds has added greater complexity to the pattern of their diversity and macroevolution, demonstrating the intertwined evolution of coloration with feather functions across display, thermoregulation, and other uses (Li et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; Terrill and Shultz, 2023).
evidence: The text cites multiple studies supporting this claim about the evolution of coloration and feather functions.

claim: Convergence in iridescent feathers exists among non-avialan theropods.
source: This linkage among colors, structures, and functions early in feather evolution extends even to convergence in iridescent feathers among non-avialan theropods, and it is highly suggestive of commonalities shared among stem and crown birds in terms of their use of colored pigments for camouflage, structural strength, and display (Hu et al., 2018; Foth and Rauhut, 2020).
evidence: The text cites studies documenting convergence in iridescent feathers among non-avialan theropods.

claim: Fossilized melanosomes have produced patterns of black, brown, rufous, gray, and other colors.
source: In a comparative setting with the melanosome feather coloration of living birds, workers have endeavored to reconstruct the colors of fossil feathers using quantitative means focused predominantly on melanosome geometry and density, and the results point to the fossilized melanosomes having produced patterns of black, brown, rufous, gray, and other colors (Vinther et al., 2008; Li et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; Li et al., 2012; Peteya et al., 2017; Benton et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites multiple studies that have reconstructed these color patterns from fossil melanosomes.

claim: The specific shape and arrangement of some fossilized feather melanosomes from non-avialan theropod dinosaurs and birds are similar to those required for producing structurally based iridescent feather coloration in living birds.
source: Furthermore, the specific shape and arrangement of some fossilized feather melanosomes derived from both non-avialan theropod dinosaurs and birds are similar to those required for producing structurally based iridescent feather coloration in living birds, a case of independent evolution (Stoddard and Prum, 2011; Hu et al., 2018; Pan et al., 2022).
evidence: The text cites studies showing similarity between fossil and living bird melanosomes for iridescence.

claim: Birds can behaviorally control their signaling through the erection of feathered ornaments such as the head crest in hoopoes or peacock tails.
source: While the display of most colored feathers is passive and available to any viewer, birds can behaviorally control their signaling through: the erection of feathered ornaments such as the head crest in hoopoes (Upupa) or peacock (Pavo) tails; the exposure of normally hidden brightly colored crown feathers as in kinglets (Regulus); and even the refined control of the black and iridescent coloration in birds such as hummingbirds (Trochilidae) and birds of paradise (Paradisaeidae; Zi et al., 2003; Wilts et al., 2014; Stoddard et al., 2020).
evidence: The text cites studies documenting behavioral control of feather displays in living birds.

claim: The variety of mixed structural colors in a peacock feather is achieved through changes in the spacing in the keratinous matrix and melanosome organization.
source: For example, the variety of mixed structural colors present in a peacock feather is achieved through changes in the spacing in the keratinous matrix and melanosome organization (Zi et al., 2003).
evidence: The text cites a study explaining the mechanism of peacock feather coloration.

claim: Hummingbirds can see non-spectral colors.
source: In addition to the normal range of spectral coloration, hummingbirds can see non-spectral colors as well, and their utility is supported by vision perception experiments (Stoddard et al., 2020).
evidence: The text cites a study demonstrating hummingbird vision capabilities.

claim: The sampled crest feather is well-preserved and comprised of elongate and relatively wide barbs.
source: The overall shape of the sampled crest feather is well-preserved and comprised of elongate and relatively wide barbs.
evidence: The text describes the morphology of the sampled feather based on direct observation.

claim: The dominant barb length is proportionally longer than the feather barb examined from the neck and head region of Confuciusornis.
source: The dominant barb length is proportionally longer than the feather barb examined from the neck and head region of Confuciusornis (Foth, 2012).
evidence: The text compares the barb length to another fossil bird species, citing a reference.

claim: The feather is defined as a barb-dominant feather, since most of the exposed feather tissue is composed of long barbs with a very short and thick calamus.
source: The feather is different from the bilaterally symmetric plumulaceous feathers of living birds, and we define it as a barb-dominant feather, since most of the exposed feather tissue is composed of long barbs with a very short and thick calamus.
evidence: The text provides a definition based on observed morphological characteristics.

claim: The feather correlates with evolutionary stage II and IIIa of Prum and Brush, 2002.
source: It is estimated to correlate with evolutionary stage II and IIIa of Prum and Brush, 2002, similar to the intermediate feather type proposed as found in an amber fossil (Perrichot et al., 2008).
evidence: The text estimates the evolutionary stage based on comparison with published feather evolution models.

claim: The new feather is distinct from the amber feather in showing an asymmetric shape, radically diverging toward one side (caudal side), and is much larger in size.
source: The new feather described here is distinct from the amber feather in showing an asymmetric shape, radically diverging toward one side (caudal side), and is much larger in size (Perrichot et al., 2008).
evidence: The text compares the fossil feather to an amber fossil, citing differences in morphology.

claim: Ultrathin histological sectioning and application of SEM and S/TEM imaging resulted in the identification of partially interlinked melanosomes with a derived asymmetric packing pattern.
source: Ultrathin histological sectioning and application of SEM and S/TEM imaging of the fossil feather samples (see Appendix  1) resulted in the identification of partially interlinked melanosomes with a derived asymmetric packing pattern (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: The text describes the results of microscopy techniques, referencing figures showing the data.

claim: The long axial crack in Figure 2 may represent the surface of the barbs, resembling a crack formed in maturation experiments.
source: The long axial crack in Figure 2 may represent the surface of the barbs, resembling a crack formed in maturation experiments (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: The text interprets a feature in Figure 2 by comparison with experimental results.

claim: Melanosome clusters are present and concentrated mostly within the barbs rather than in the barbules of extant bird feathers based on similar size.
source: Those melanosome clusters are present and concentrated mostly within the barbs rather than in the barbules of extant bird feathers based on similar size (Figure 2).

source: The long axis of the densely packed melanosomes is aligned overall parallel with the barb's long axis (Figure 2), which has been confirmed by detailed histological data as well.

source: The melanosomes are arranged in an asymmetric hexagonal conformation, clearly visible in the different sections (see Figure 3).

claim: The thickness of the complete feather barb with filled melanosomes is around 10 µm.
source: The thickness of the complete feather barb with filled melanosomes (preserved) is around 10 µm, which is much greater than the typical diameter of known barbules, but similar to barbs in extant birds (Freyer et al., 2021).
evidence: The text provides a measurement of barb thickness and compares it to extant birds.

claim: Hooks are commonly observed on the oval-shaped melanosomes in cross-sectional views, with two dominant types identified on the dorsal and ventral sides.
source: Hooks are commonly observed on the oval-shaped melanosomes in cross-sectional views, with two dominant types identified on the dorsal and ventral sides (Figure 3c–d, red arrows).
evidence: The text describes hook structures visible in Figure 3.

claim: The major axis (y) of the oval-shaped melanosomes has a mean of 283 nm.
source: The major axis (y) of the oval-shaped melanosomes (mean = 283 nm) is oriented toward the left side in cross-section, while the shorter axis (x) measures approximately 186 nm (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: The text provides measurements of melanosome dimensions, referencing a table.

claim: The shorter axis (x) of the oval-shaped melanosomes measures approximately 186 nm.
source: The major axis (y) of the oval-shaped melanosomes (mean = 283 nm) is oriented toward the left side in cross-section, while the shorter axis (x) measures approximately 186 nm (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: The text provides measurements of melanosome dimensions, referencing a table.

claim: The hooked structures enhance the structural integrity of the barb.
source: Based on these observations, we propose that the hooked structures—particularly those on the dorsal, ventral, proximal, and distal sides of the melanosomes—enhance the structural integrity of the barb (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: The text proposes a functional interpretation of the hook structures based on observations.

source: These hooks may stabilize the stacked melanosome rods and contribute to increased barb dimensions, such as diameter and length.

claim: The long rod-like melanosomes are different from all other known feather melanosomes from both extant and extinct taxa in having some extra hooks and an oblique ellipse shape in cross and longitudinal sections.
source: The long rod-like melanosomes are different from all other known feather melanosomes from both extant and extinct taxa in having some extra hooks and an oblique ellipse shape in cross and longitudinal sections of individual melanosomes (Durrer, 1986; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: The text compares the fossil melanosomes to known examples, citing references.

claim: The asymmetric packing of the melanosomes played a major role in the reduction of fossilized keratinous matrix within the barbs.
source: The asymmetric packing of the melanosomes (the major axis leans leftward in cross section) played a major role in the reduction of fossilized keratinous matrix within the barbs, which may correspond to a novel structural coloration in this extinct bird.
evidence: The text proposes a relationship between melanosome packing and keratin matrix reduction.

claim: The asymmetric compact hexagonal packing (ACHP) of the melanosomes is different from the known pattern of melanosomes formed in the structure of barbules among extant birds.
source: The asymmetric compact hexagonal packing (ACHP) of the melanosomes is different from the known pattern of melanosomes formed in the structure of barbules among extant birds (Eliason and Shawkey, 2012), which has been seen as a regular hexagonal organization.

claim: When light is incident at a small angle (≤30°, both s- and p-polarized) in the X-Y plane, no evident reflection peak was found in the visible spectrum.
source: In the computational (FDTD) simulation, when light is incident at a small angle (≤30°, both s- and p-polarized) in the X-Y plane, no evident reflection peak was found in the visible spectrum, as shown in Figure 4c (e.g. when a viewer observes at this angle, the light is almost completely absorbed, and the crest feather would have a darkened appearance).
evidence: The text describes results from FDTD modeling shown in Figure 4c.

claim: As the incident angle varies from 40° to 70°, the wavelength corresponding to the reflection peak shifts from 687 nm to 475 nm, and the color of the reflection peak gradually changes from red to deep blue.
source: As the incident angle varies from 40° to 70°, the wavelength corresponding to the reflection peak shifts from 687 nm to 475 nm, and the color of the reflection peak gradually changes from red to deep blue (inset in Figure 4c clearly shows how the resulting color varies with the angle of incidence).
evidence: The text describes modeling results showing angle-dependent color changes, referencing Figure 4c.

claim: The generation of iridescent color is caused by the constructive interference between scattered light produced by these uniquely shaped melanosomes that are compactly arranged in the barbs.
source: From the perspective of optical modeling, the generation of iridescent color (reflection peaks in the visible spectrum) is caused by the constructive interference between scattered light produced by these uniquely shaped melanosomes that are compactly arranged in the barbs (Vinther et al., 2010).
evidence: The text explains the physical mechanism of iridescence, citing a reference.

claim: The three-dimensional multilayer nanostructure model is somehow equivalent to one-dimensional multilayer biphotonic crystals.

evidence: The text draws a comparison to biphotonic crystals, citing a reference.

claim: The crest feather of the Cretaceous enantiornithine shows a strikingly angle-dependent and iridescent coloration pattern.

source: The recognition of overall iridescence links to a commonly found extant bird color range only known previously from the platelet-shaped dinosaurian melanosomes (Hu et al., 2018) and a few fossil feathers (Pan et al., 2022; Nordén et al., 2019; Nordén et al., 2021).

source: The independent evolution of overall iridescence, similar to that found in living birds, was reconstructed here based on a novel array of melanosomes in a feather barb in an extinct non-crown group bird (Nordén et al., 2019; Yoshioka and Akiyama, 2021).
evidence: The text interprets the findings as evidence of independent evolution, citing references.

claim: The occurrence of iridescent structural coloration in an enlarged head crest on this ancient bird is similar to structures present across many living birds that employ iridescence for intimidation, signaling, and particularly for mate attraction or intraspecific territorial defense.
source: The occurrence of iridescent structural coloration in an enlarged head crest on this ancient bird is similar to structures present across many living birds that employ iridescence for intimidation, signaling, and particularly for mate attraction or intraspecific territorial defense (Terrill and Shultz, 2023).

claim: This individual bird likely was a male based on the occurrence of paired rachis dominant tail feathers.
source: Given that this individual bird likely was a male based on the occurrence of paired rachis dominant tail feathers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), the vibrant coloration on a prominent feathered crest suggests that sexual selection may have long played an important role in avialan (feather) macroevolution (Foth, 2020; Wang et al., 2021).

claim: Sexual selection may have long played an important role in avialan (feather) macroevolution.
source: Given that this individual bird likely was a male based on the occurrence of paired rachis dominant tail feathers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), the vibrant coloration on a prominent feathered crest suggests that sexual selection may have long played an important role in avialan (feather) macroevolution (Foth, 2020; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: The text proposes a role for sexual selection based on the findings, citing references.

source: Our discovery of new melanosome shapes and networks suggests that birds evolved previously unrecognized patterns of color production outside of the limits present among crown group birds.

source: Additionally, these pigments and their dense organization may have made the foundation of the feather darker and allowed for a more intense or vibrant iridescent coloration, a potential relationship that is understudied among living birds.

source: While the interrelationship between melanin content in feathers and increases in structural strength have long been known (Burtt, 1981; Burtt and Ichida, 2004), perhaps the increased density of melanosomes in this fossil feather barbs added even more structural strength to the feathered crest of this bird in compromise for its lack of a dominant rachis.
evidence: The text cites established knowledge about melanin and structural strength.

claim: The increased density of melanosomes in this fossil feather barbs may have added structural strength to the feathered crest in compromise for its lack of a dominant rachis.
source: While the interrelationship between melanin content in feathers and increases in structural strength have long been known (Burtt, 1981; Burtt and Ichida, 2004), perhaps the increased density of melanosomes in this fossil feather barbs added even more structural strength to the feathered crest of this bird in compromise for its lack of a dominant rachis.

source: Additionally, the interlocking hooks among the melanosomes might have aided individual feather barb in resisting shear forces.

source: Size reduction in melanosomes was found previously in a simulation experiment (McNamara et al., 2013), but such a reduction is very unlikely to result in the highly organized and consistent melanosome packing present here (McNamara et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2020).

source: Given the lack of barbules in most early primitive feather forms (or filamentary structures) in non-avialan dinosaurs and pterosaurs, the positioning of melanosomes in barbs might be a plesiomorphic feature for ornithodirans broadly (Xu, 2019; Cincotta et al., 2022).

source: Here, we recovered iridescent coloration in fossil bird feathers that was produced by three-dimensional melanosome packing patterns. This discovery dramatically expands the range of fossil bird coloration space, and this diversity in feather coloration in an early bird fits well with its forested environment, as proposed by the coeval fossil plant community (Wu et al., 2023).

This additional modeling resulted in all of the spectral peaks present in the original modeling being recovered.
